lead: This unit is about the Linux file system as you meet it from the shell: the tree of directories, the commands that list, read, copy, move, link and delete files, and the permission bits that decide who may touch them. After it you can read an ls -l line field by field, predict whether an operation will be refused, and set modes and owners so the right people get access.
about: This unit treats the file system as a working tool, not as kernel code. Chapter 2.1 maps the directory tree and the file types, so a path like /home/ravi/lab/notes.txt stops being a string and becomes a route. Chapter 2.2 uses ls, cat, more and less to list and read what the tree holds. Chapter 2.3 changes the tree: mkdir, cp, mv, rm, hard and soft links, and find to search it. Chapter 2.4 explains the ten permission characters and chmod, and 2.5 adds owners, groups and the order in which the kernel checks them. After the unit you can read any listing, say why a command was refused, and fix the mode instead of guessing.

chapters.idea: The Linux file system is one tree under /, and every entry in it is one of a small set of file types.
chapters.depth: Top-level directories of the hierarchy (bin, boot, dev, etc, home, lib, proc, root, tmp, usr, var) and what each holds. Absolute and relative paths, and how the kernel walks a path component by component. The seven file types read from the first character of an ls -l line: - regular, d directory, l symbolic link, c character device, b block device, p named pipe, s socket. One line each on inode numbers and on virtual file systems such as /proc and /sys. Some syllabi call the directory layout the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS).

figure.aria: A tree of the root directory showing the standard top-level directories and two example subdirectories below them.
figure.title: The tree under /

chapters.example:
A directory listing shows four lines:
-rw-r--r-- 1 ravi students 2148 Jan  5 10:20 notes.txt
drwxr-xr-x 2 ravi students 4096 Jan  5 09:00 lab
lrwxrwxrwx 1 ravi students    9 Jan  4 18:02 latest -> notes.txt
crw--w---- 1 root tty      4,   1 Jan  5 08:00 tty1
For each line give the file type, explain why the link count is 1, 2, 1 and 1, and say what the number 2148 counts. Then, standing in /home/ravi, give the absolute path reached by ../ravi/lab/latest and the type of the final file after the link is followed.
chapters.trap: The first character is the file type, not a permission, so a leading d or l does not mean 'no permission'. Also, the number before the date on a device file is major,minor, not a byte count.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: kernel, shell and user space, and the basic command line.
chapters.leave: Inode internals, block groups, ext2 layout and the implementation of /proc → Unit 5.

chapters.idea: ls lists what exists, and cat, more and less show what is inside, each suited to a different file size.
chapters.depth: ls with -l, -a, -h, -R, -t, -r, -i, -d, -F, and how the shell expands wildcards like *.c before ls ever runs. Reading the seven fields of a long listing. cat with -n, -A, -s and why it floods a terminal. more and less and their key presses (space, b, G, /, ?, q), and why less is preferred on large files because it does not load the whole file. lpr and the print queue in one line. Name tac, head and tail as relatives in one line. Some syllabi list this as 'listing files' and 'displaying files'.

figure.aria: A block diagram of one file opened by four tools: cat prints it all, more pages forward, less moves both ways and searches, lpr sends it to a printer.
figure.title: One file, four ways to look at it

chapters.example:
/home/ravi/lab holds notes.txt (2148 bytes), big.log (5,242,880 bytes), the hidden file .profile, and one subdirectory reports that holds two files.
(a) Write the command that lists every entry, hidden ones included, with sizes in human units. How many lines does it print?
(b) Write the command that lists the entry reports itself, not its contents.
(c) Show notes.txt with line numbers.
(d) Page through big.log, jump to the last line, then search backwards for ERROR.
(e) What size does ls -lh print for big.log?
chapters.trap: ls -l on a directory prints the directory's contents, never the directory's own details; use -d. And -h divides by 1024, so 5,242,880 bytes prints as 5.0M, not 5.2M.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 for the tree and the file types.
chapters.leave: Pipes, redirection and grep/sed/awk on the output → Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Copying, moving, linking and deleting all act on directory entries, and the inode underneath decides what survives.
chapters.depth: Directory work with mkdir -p, rmdir, cd, pwd and touch. cp with -r, -p, -i, -u, -d; mv as rename inside a file system and as copy-then-delete across file systems; rm with -r, -f, -i, and why rm -rf has no undo. Hard links and symbolic links: link count, dangling links, what a symlink stores, and why a hard link cannot cross a file system. find with -name, -type, -size, -mtime, -perm, -exec and -delete, plus the habit of testing with -print first. Tar archiving gets one line here.

figure.aria: A graph showing one inode reached by two names with link count 2, and a symbolic link on a separate inode that stores the first name as text.

chapters.example:
/home/ravi and /home/ravi/work sit on the same file system. The file notes.txt in /home/ravi has inode 1042 and 300 bytes.
Step 1: ln notes.txt hard.txt
Step 2: ln -s notes.txt soft.txt
Step 3: rm notes.txt
(a) Give the link count of inode 1042 after each step.
(b) What does cat hard.txt print after step 3, and why?
(c) What does cat soft.txt print after step 3?
(d) Write a find command that lists regular files under /home/ravi larger than 1 MB and modified in the last 7 days.
(e) Then run mv hard.txt work/. Does the inode number change?
chapters.trap: rm removes a name and lowers the link count; the data goes only when the count reaches 0. Students also forget that mv across file systems copies and deletes, so the inode does change.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2.1 and 2.2: the tree, file types and the long listing.
chapters.leave: Regular expressions for matching names, and text processing on find output → Unit 3; device files and file system layout → Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Ten characters and three octal digits fully describe what an owner, a group and everyone else may do to a file.
chapters.depth: The ten mode characters and what r, w, x mean for a regular file (read, write, execute) versus a directory (list names, create or delete entries, enter or traverse). chmod in octal and in symbolic form with u, g, o, a and +, -, =. umask and the default modes 666 for files and 777 for directories. Why execute on a directory gates everything inside it. SUID, SGID and the sticky bit in short; only a few universities teach these in this unit, and the sticky bit is what keeps /tmp usable.

figure.title: chmod 754 on notes.txt: - rwx r-x r--

chapters.aria: An array of the ten mode characters with the octal value of each r, w and x position written below it, adding to 754.
chapters.example:
notes.txt shows -rw-r--r-- and is owned by ravi.
(a) Give two commands, one octal and one symbolic, that change it to rwxr-x--- .
(b) With umask set to 022, what mode does touch a.txt give a new file, and what mode does mkdir d give a new directory?
(c) A user with umask 022 wants new files to come out as 640 instead of 644. What must the umask be?
(d) The directory lab is drwxr-x--- and the file lab/report.txt inside it is -rw-r--r--. priya is not ravi and is not in ravi's group. Can she read report.txt?
chapters.trap: (d) is the classic: the other bits on report.txt say read, but without x on lab she cannot traverse the directory, so the open fails. Students also subtract the umask from the wrong base number.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.2 for the long listing, chapter 2.3 for creating test files.
chapters.leave: ACLs and per-user grants → chapter 2.5; creating and deleting user accounts → Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Every file has one owner and one group, and the kernel checks root, then owner, then group, then other, and stops at the first match.
chapters.depth: uid and gid, root as uid 0, and the fields of /etc/passwd and /etc/group. Primary versus supplementary groups, and why group membership is the usual way to share files in a lab. chown and chgrp, including -R. id, whoami, groups and newgrp. The order of the permission check and why a user who is the owner never falls through to the other bits. ACLs with getfacl and setfacl: only a few universities teach this, so keep it to the idea of a per-user grant.

figure.title: Which bits decide
figure.aria: A flowchart of the permission check: root is allowed at once, otherwise the owner bits, then the group bits, then the other bits decide.

chapters.example:
/home/ravi/project/report.txt is owned by ravi, group students, mode 640. The users are: ravi (uid 1001, primary group ravi, also in students), priya (uid 1002, groups priya and students), arjun (uid 1003, group arjun).
(a) For priya and arjun, say read, write, execute allowed or denied, and which triplet decided it.
(b) root runs cat report.txt. Allowed? Why?
(c) Write the command that changes the file's group to arjun.
(d) After (c), who can read it: priya or arjun? What did the students get and lose?
(e) Give a better way to let arjun read it without moving the group.
chapters.trap: Students check the other bits for a user who is actually in the file's group, and forget that one user is matched by exactly one triplet. Root bypasses file permissions; it is not 'allowed by the owner bits'.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.4 for the permission bits and chmod.
chapters.leave: Adding and removing users and groups, sudo rules, password aging → Unit 4.
